If I try to use 

import Mathlib
def bad : ℕ :=
  ∑ i in Finset.range 5, i

I currently get
unexpected token 'in'; expected ','

and the code won't run. I think I am missing something to do with big notation, but I'm really lost on this one. I'm currently on
Lean (version 4.30.0-rc2, x86_64-w64-windows-gnu, commit 3dc1a088b6d2d8eafe25a7cd7ec7b58d731bd7cc, Release)
Lake version 5.0.0-src+3dc1a08 (Lean version 4.30.0-rc2)
leanprover/lean4-nightly:nightly-2026-04-28
leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2

Which is probably part of the problem, too, I imagine.

This works:

import Mathlib
def bad : ℕ :=
  ∑ i ∈ Finset.range 5, i
Out of curiosity, where did you get the in syntax? We removed it a while back

I'm too new to Lean and formal proofs in general, so I am forced to use an AI assistant to help me formalize my mathematics. It makes mistakes, and they are hard to catch because I am so new to this language.

The only reason that it is even possible, is that Lean type-checks. But it can sneak other problems in. Debugging is hell.

Ian Allen said:

I am forced to use an AI assistant

Why do you think this?

Because my need to complete a formalization of my theory supersedes my need to learn the language entirely on my own. I am learning as I go as it is, I certainly would learn more if I did everything entirely myself, but it would take years to make the progress I have.

I can do most of the math on paper, other parts I just have a natural intuition about the shape of things. Lean has been very helpful in uncovering some small holes in the assumptions, but in general what I write down in my own workbook is correct. Unfortunately, that is not enough if I am trying to speak to other mathematicians. So while I can for example write a couple large formulas down and say "this is clearly a bijection" (I would have just said they both encompass the same problem entirely but my personal language is entirely informal, I have learned from Lean), I am forced to prove that in lean, and that's currently well above my grade. Showing the various mappings are bijective is just a cornerstone of my theory, so if I want to actually get any work done, now preferably, I need to use an AI to accelerate the process.

Forced is perhaps a strong word. I am guilty of exaggeration. But the need is there.

With where AI is right now, it is exactly what you should not follow when learning Lean (or any new programming language), because as you said, it can make mistakes, and you don't know how to correct it.

Well.. I'm mostly using it to formalize my work. Learning is just a side bonus, and here I learn as much from the AI's mistakes as I do its correctness, probably more so because if a lemma works, there's not a big incentive for me right now to dig into it, other than the usual rigor of making certain there are no assumptions (hand-waved definitions), everything is derived, and everything is connected to the logical pipeline correctly, and of course that the statement and the result are sound in the framework of my project.

I don't have an encyclopedic knowledge of Mathlib yet, nor do I fully understand the tactics. Just the syntax alone of this language is like reading hieroglyphics to me. But I am picking it up, and I am also understanding the meta level of coding in lean -the administrative level if you will, which is quite important just to get a project moving.

But I'm not arguing with anybody here on the point: it would be far superior to dig into lean at a fundamental level and learn it from the ground up, if learning lean was my primary goal right now. It's not. It's a secondary goal and I will take it up with rigor when I have completed my current work, which is nearly done.

" ... and you don't know how to correct it."
If that was perfectly true, I would absolutely agree with you. But it's not.

I'm not sure what the benefit of formalizing your math is if you cannot do it yourself. Are you trying to get Lean to check the math?

You don't have to go all the way down to the fundamental level of Lean's type theory, but it's a very healthy thing to get to know what the formalized library knows and how it all fits together. (And then there comes a time where things are done at a higher level of generality than you were expecting, so that it's hard to follow again)

I think it's important to underline that, as I was saying to Weiyi Wang, my comprehension of lean is not binary. It's not: you understand nothing, or you understand. I'm in the middle, sure on the lower end, but I am learning. That's an important distinction, and AI helps me to increase that comprehension. I also don't really have anybody else who will sit with me 12+ hours a day and answer questions, more's the pity.

So I can do more and more myself, each day. That's a good thing. Am I trying to get Lean to check the math? Sure why not? That is one aspect, and I would be highly doubtful if you didn't say that was a primary aspect of using lean for pretty much anybody. Everybody makes mistakes, and lean finds a certain important class of them (type errors) which cuts down significantly on the overhead of "did I make a mistake, I'd better double or triple check my math."

Lean (and the AI) is also useful as a tool to advance my level of mathematics. AI teaches me outright concepts and patterns, all of which are easily cross referenced with a standard, static resource, and lean is absolute magic for finding your assumptive mistakes. Does a lemma refuse to type-check? First I ask the AI to reconfirm with me what the goal is and what it's plan is, and I can quickly deduce if the AI has drifted into "undefined" or outright incorrect territory. If the AI seems to be doing the job correctly, eventually I can come to an understanding of what the goal is which the AI is stuck on, and this gives enormous insights into exactly the problem of erroneous assumptions or just arithmetic mistakes on my part. I've uncovered several "holes" in my theory (all of which I could quickly correct for) in this manner.

I think finally, using lean is hopefully a way to build some level of credibility. If you are working on a difficult problem, and you are unknown in the community, the kneejerk reaction (I have learned) among professional mathematicians is, unfortunately, almost immediate disregard. "The person is a crack-pot", or equivalently, "the person is a waste of my time." I understand that response. As a physicist, there was no end of "water can fuel cars" or "zero point energy is being buried by the government" people. It's obnoxious. It is absolutely a waste of time. The ethical difference is: In physics, these are solved problems, at least within the context of a widely accepted and deeply experimentally reinforced epistemology. You cannot, as far as we understand things, cheat thermodynamics, and if you say you can, you had better be able to bring home the bacon. To date, nobody has brought home the bacon.

In mathematics, there are problems which are generally considered exceptionally difficult. They might even be unsolvable, at least in the context of our current language and capabilities. But nobody knows this. They are not solved. So there is an ethical contradiction when mathematicians knee-jerk an entirely assumptive response about another human being, who claims to have some improved understanding of the problem. Again, it is an understandable response, but it is fundamentally problematic, and it serves to restrain advancement in the admittedly rare cases where a person does have something of importance to share.

The problem I am working on, is to a large extent self-correcting; I can most often easily see if the math goes astray, because the results are immediately errant. I can tell if the AI is astray, because the work in Lean drags to a standstill, and Lean refuses to compile, in most cases, a non-truth. Ultimately, I can tell if I am astray, and I can then rectify the problem. I can also use lean to discover new truths in this context; truly it is an amazing tool. But my point here is, I have spent years working on this project, and I believe that my work is correct, and lean strongly reinforces this belief.

So for all of these reasons, I am codifying my theories into lean. I am very, very nearly complete in my project. Everything compiles, and everything in lean agrees with my personal understanding. The ironic thing is, after having done all of this work, will the community simply kick the "crackpot" can down the road, and assume I (using AI) must have made a mistake in the code? And more importantly, can I ever be satisfied in myself, that I "truly know something" and haven't made a mistake? Can anyone?

Lean is a crutch in this regard; there is no absolute knowledge and we are all trapped in the same epistemological quagmire. But it sure is nice and better than the alternative, which is not having lean.

I look forward to sharing my work and hopefully, having a conversation or two about the results. I hope people will spare some of their truly invaluable time for it.
